newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer says ERM link needed for EMU membership.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer says ERM link needed for EMU membership.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer on Thursday reiterated that membership of Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) was essential for participation in the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
"The Treaty is very clear on this point. Membership in ERM is a condition," Tietmeyer told Swedish reporters at a press meeting.
Sweden, like fellow EU members Britain and Italy and does not belong to the ERM. Finland joined the ERM this week.
Under the Maastricht Treaty on European Union, countries must maintain a stable currency for two years prior to the decision on which countries qualify for monetary union.

Countries must also stick to limits set for the budget deficit, public borrowing as well as long-term interest rates and inflation. The decision on which EU states can launch monetary union in 1999 will be based on their data for 1997.
But Sweden and Britain have repeatedly said that linking their currencies to the ERM was not on the agenda and not a prerequisite for joining EMU.
Sweden's Prime Minister Goran Persson and Finance Minister Erik Asbrink have maintained that the important condition for EMU membership is stability in the currency itself, not the link to the ERM.

The difference of opinion appears to stem from Europe's currency upheaval in 1993 which forced sterling and the lira out of the ERM and led to a widening of the bands within which currencies trade against each other.
Those bands were expanded to as wide as 15 percent from the 2.25 percent which applied when the Treaty was signed.

The mark and the Dutch guilder, still trading within the old 2.25 percent bands, are the only exceptions to the ERM arrangement in which the currencies of nine countries fluctuate within 15 percent of agreed central rates against other members.
The Bundesbank has been at the forefront in stressing that all entry criteria must be strictly maintained to ensure that the euro will be at least as stable as the mark.
Tietmeyer said countries must prove they can fulfil criteria in a sustainable way.

"In my opinion and according to the treaty a country has to show that it can keep the exchange rate stable for a long time but we also have to see if a country fulfils the criteria in a sustainable way," he said.
He said there were good possibilities for the two key countries, France and Germany, to fulfil EMU participation requirements.
"I think we have a good possibilty even if we are not entirely certain. Both countries may need additional adjustment measures," he added.
Tietmeyer also said no country could be forced into the union and other member states would have to wait for the outcome of the political debate in Sweden.
"I don't think other EU countries can force another country to fulfil the criteria," he said.
"I think I understand the political debate in Sweden but we will just have to wait and see what the outcome is."
President of the European Monetary Institute, Alexandre Lamfalussy, said on Monday that Sweden would do well to play it by the book.

"My opinion is that a country should be in the ERM for two years before it can enter the EMU and that's the interpretation of the majority (of countries) of the convergence criteria," Lamfalussy said during a visit to Sweden this week.
